The etymology is not entirely certain; it is probably a fusion of Middle English swam (“swamp, muddy pool, bog, marsh”, also “fungus, mushroom”) — from Old English swamm (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz — and M

gloss: To drench or fill with water.
etymology: Early attestations (starting in 1624) are from North America, but the term was probably in local use in Britain earlier. The etymology is not entirely certain; it is probably a fusion of Middle English swam (“swamp, muddy pool, bog, marsh”, also “fungus, mushroom”) — from Old English swamm (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz — and M

gloss: Earth which grass has grown into the upper layer of; greensward, sod, turf; (countable) a portion of such earth.
etymology:
The noun is derived from Middle English sward (“rind; skin; calloused skin; leather strap; sod, turf”) [and other forms], from Old English sweard, swearð (“rind; skin”), from Proto-Germanic *swarduz (“rind; tough skin; turf”); further etymology unknown.
The verb is derived from the noun.

gloss: To cover (ground, etc.) with sward.
etymology:
The noun is derived from Middle English sward (“rind; skin; calloused skin; leather strap; sod, turf”) [and other forms], from Old English sweard, swearð (“rind; skin”), from Proto-Germanic *swarduz (“rind; tough skin; turf”); further etymology unknown.
The verb is derived from the noun.

gloss: A piece, pattern, or sample, generally of cloth or a similar material.
etymology: From earlier Northern England dialectal swache (“the counterfoil or counterstock of a tally”) (1512); further etymology unknown. Cognate with Scots swach, swatch. Compare English swath, swathe. Compare also Old English swæcc (“taste; flavour; odour; fragrance”).

gloss: To create a swatch, especially a sample of knitted fabric.
etymology: From earlier Northern England dialectal swache (“the counterfoil or counterstock of a tally”) (1512); further etymology unknown. Cognate with Scots swach, swatch. Compare English swath, swathe. Compare also Old English swæcc (“taste; flavour; odour; fragrance”).

gloss: The track cut out by a scythe in mowing.
etymology: From Middle English swath, swathe, from Old English swæþ, swaþu (“track; trace; footstep”), from Proto-Germanic *swaþō (“a wind-swept place; open field”), of unknown further origin. Has been derived from a Proto-Indo-European *swey- (“to bend, turn, swing”), and compared with Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “snub-nosed”) and Welsh chwil (“reeling, staggering”), though this is uncertain, as well as the

gloss: To become bigger, especially due to being engorged.
etymology:
From Middle English swellen, from Old English swellan (“to swell”), from Proto-West Germanic *swellan, from Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”), of unknown origin.
Cognate with Saterland Frisian swälle (“to swell”), West Frisian swolle (“to swell”), Dutch zwellen (“to swell”), Low German swellen (“to swell”), German schwellen (“to swell”), Swedish svälla (“to swell”), Icelandic svella. The adjec

gloss: Any of various kinds of alcoholic drink.
etymology:
Unknown etymology, 1813. Original sense “alcoholic drink”, possibly a variant of switchel (“a drink of molasses and water, often mixed with rum”), attested 1790, itself of uncertain origin. Possibly influenced by swirl or fizz.
In verb sense “to stir”, from swizzle stick (“stick for stirring alcoholic drinks”), itself attested 1859.

gloss: A drink dating back to the 16th century consisting primarily of milk curdled with an alcoholic beverage or some acid such as lemon juice, which is usually then sweetened and spiced.
etymology: Origin unknown; the spelling may have been influenced by the unrelated word syllable.

gloss: A small flap or strip of material attached to or inserted into something, for holding, manipulation, identification, opening etc.
etymology: First attested 1607, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A small nail with a flat head.
etymology: From Middle English tak, takke (“hook; staple; nail”), from Old Northern French taque (“nail, pin, peg”), from Frankish *takkō, from Proto-Germanic *takkô (“tip; point; protrusion; prong; tine; jag; spike; twig”), of unknown origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dHgʰ-n-, from the root *déHgʰ- (“to pinch; to tear, rip, fray”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Takke (“bough; branch; twig”), W

gloss: A Mexican snack food made of a small tortilla (soft- or hard-shelled) filled with ingredients such as meat, rice, beans, cheese, diced vegetables, and salsa.
etymology: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish taco, of uncertain origin; see the Spanish entry for more.

gloss: An earthenware cooking pot of North African origin, consisting of a shallow, round dish without handles and a tall, conical or dome-shaped lid.
etymology: From Moroccan Arabic طَجِين (ṭajīn), from Arabic طَاجِن (ṭājin, “shallow earthen pot”), from Ancient Greek τάγηνον (tágēnon, “frying pan, saucepan”), further etymology unknown.

gloss: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see take, with.
etymology: From a substrate of Germanic immigrant languages to the Midwest that feature the same construction. Compare German mitnehmen and Swedish ta med.

gloss: A repeated rhythmic pattern used in isorhythm.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin talea, of uncertain origin. Possibly connected with Latin tālea (“cutting; scion”).

gloss: A culinary strainer, originally made from worsted cloth.
etymology:
Borrowed from French tamis, from Middle French tamis, from Old French tamis, from Medieval Latin tamisium, of unclear origin.
Cognate with Old High German zemis (dialectal German Zims), Dutch teems (“sieve”), West Frisian teams, tiems, German Low German Teemse, Teems, Old English temes, Old English temesian (“to sieve; sift”). Doublet of temse.

gloss: An alpha-adrenergic blocking agent administered orally in the form of its hydrochloride C₂₀H₂₈N₂O₅S·HCl to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia.
etymology: From tam- (of unknown origin) + sul(fonamide) + -osin (“α₁-adrenoceptor antagonist”).

gloss: A large drinking vessel, sometimes of pewter, sometimes with a glass base, with one handle and often a hinged cover.
etymology:
From Middle English tan(c)kard(e), denoting 'a large tub for carrying liquid', perhaps related to Dutch tanckaert, from Middle Dutch tanckaert, meaning the same thing, but of uncertain ultimate origin. The OED suggests an alteration of Medieval Latin *kantard, from Latin cantharus (“tankard”). Klein suggests French tant quart (“as much of a quarter”).
Meaning "drinking vessel" is first recorded la

gloss: An often childish display or fit of bad temper.
etymology: From earlier tanterum. Further etymology unknown.

gloss: To throw a tantrum.
etymology: From earlier tanterum. Further etymology unknown.

gloss: To make thinner or narrower at one end.
etymology: From Middle English taper, from Old English tapor (“taper, candle, wick of a lamp”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Latin papyrus (“papyrus", used in Mediaeval times to mean "wick of a candle”). If so, it is a doublet of papyrus. gloss: A piece of paper given to students who are late to class.
etymology: From an earlier tardive, from French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus (“slow”, “sluggish”), of obscure origin.

gloss: A type of small open pie, or piece of pastry, now typically containing jelly (US) / jam (UK) or conserve, or sometimes other fillings (chocolate, custard, egg, butter, historically even meat or other
etymology: From Middle English tart, tarte, from Old French tarte, tartre (“flat pastry”) (compare Medieval Latin tarta), of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of Old French torte, tourte, from Latin turta, perhaps from tŏrta f (“twisted”), in which case it would be cognate to torta.

gloss: Any of various small freshwater ducks of the genus Anas that are brightly coloured and have short necks.
etymology: From Middle English tele, probably from an unrecorded Old English *tǣle, cognate with West Frisian tjilling (“teal”), Middle Dutch teling (“teal”) (modern Dutch taling), Middle Low German telink, from Proto-Germanic *tailijaz, of unknown ultimate origin, with no cognates outside of Germanic. As the name of a shade of dark greenish-blue like the color patterns on the fowl's head and wings, it is at

gloss: To kindle; ignite; set on fire; light; inflame; burn.
etymology: From Middle English tenden, from Old English tendan (“to kindle, set on fire”) (usually in compounds ātendan, fortendan, ontendan), from Proto-Germanic *tandijaną (“to kindle”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Danish tænde (“to kindle”), Swedish tända (“to ignite”), Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (tandjan, “to kindle”), Icelandic tendra (“to ignite”), German zünden (“to light, ignite, fire”). Related to tinder.

gloss: A Mediterranean tree (Pistacia terebinthus and, possibly, Pistacia palaestina)
etymology: From Middle English therebynte, from Old French terebinthe, from Latin terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos), from Pre-Greek. Related to turpentine and terpene.

gloss: A recombinant form of parathyroid hormone, used in the treatment of some forms of osteoporosis.
etymology: From teri- (of unknown origin) + para(thyroid) + -tide (“peptide, glycopeptide”).

gloss: Any of several isomeric monoterpenoid alcohols found in the essential oil of pine and other trees
etymology: From terpentin or terpin + -ol, reduction from terebinth, ultimately from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos), from Pre-Greek.

gloss: A rope, cable etc. that holds something in place whilst allowing some movement.
etymology: From Middle English tether, teder, from Old English *tēoder and/or Old Norse tjóðr ( > Danish tøjr, Swedish tjuder); both from Proto-Germanic *teudrą (“rope; cord; shaft”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dewtro-, from Proto-Indo-European *dew- (“to tie”), or from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull”). Cognate with North German Tüder (“tether for binding the cattle”), Swedi

gloss: Something or someone excellent, surpassingly wonderful, or cool.
etymology:
Attested since 1922, of unclear origin. There are several suggested origins, but it most likely arose in imitation of the numerous animal-related nonsense phrases popular in the 1920s such as the cat's pyjamas, cat's whiskers, cat's meow, gnat's elbow, monkey's eyebrows etc.
A popular folk etymology has the phrase referring to the world champion dancer Bee Jackson. Another suggestion is that the p

gloss: A hymn to Dionysus, sung in processions in his honour.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin thriambus, from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos), of Pre-Greek origin. Doublet of triumph and trump.

gloss: The three-tiered papal crown.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára), of unknown ultimate origin.

gloss: To touch repeatedly or stroke delicately in a manner which typically causes laughter, pleasure and twitching.
etymology:
From Middle English tiklen, tikelen, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a frequentative form of Middle English tikken (“to touch lightly”), thus equivalent to tick + -le; or perhaps related to Old English tinclian (“to tickle”). Compare North Frisian tigele (“to tickle”) (Hallig dialect), and tiikle (“to tickle”) (Amrum dialect), German dialectal zicklen (“to excite; stir up”).

gloss: A bisphosphonate drug used for treatment of Paget's disease of bone.
etymology: From thi- + -lu- (of unknown origin) + -dronic (“calcium metabolism regulator”) acid.

gloss: A traditional musical instrument of the Canary Islands and Murcia, having four or more commonly five strings, and similar in size to a ukulele but with a distinctive semi-round back.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish timple, from tiple, of uncertain etymology.

gloss: To become sleepy or weary.
etymology: From Middle English tiren, tirien, teorien, from Old English tȳrian, tēorian (“to fail, cease, become weary, be tired, exhausted; tire, weary, exhaust”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *teuʀōn (“to cease”), which is possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dews- (“to fail, be behind, lag”). gloss: To walk unsteadily, as a small child does.
etymology: Of unknown origin. Possibly a byform of totter.

gloss: A wooden or metal pin, short rod, crosspiece or similar, fixed transversely in the eye of a rope or chain to be secured to any other loop, ring, or bight, e.g. a sea painter to a lifeboat.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. Possible alteration of tug (“to pull”) + -le

gloss: To alternate between two positions using a single switch or lever.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. Possible alteration of tug (“to pull”) + -le

gloss: Synonym of idiot: someone who is foolish or stupid.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish tonto (“stupid, foolish; idiot, fool”), of uncertain etymology. Originally in US use but now chiefly British. Cf. earlier Tonto, with which it is sometimes confused.

gloss: Situated on the top of something.
etymology:
From Middle English top, toppe, from Old English topp (“top, highest part; summit; crest; tassel, tuft; (spinning) top, ball; a tuft or ball at the highest point of anything”), from Proto-West Germanic *topp, from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“braid, pigtail, end”), of unknown ultimate origin.
Cognate with Saterland Frisian Top (“top”), Cimbrian sòpf (“braid”), Dutch top (“top, summit, peak”), German T

gloss: The signal among tailors and seamstresses for snuffing the candle. The last of them to cry "top" had to snuff the candle.
etymology:
From Middle English top, toppe, from Old English topp (“top, highest part; summit; crest; tassel, tuft; (spinning) top, ball; a tuft or ball at the highest point of anything”), from Proto-West Germanic *topp, from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“braid, pigtail, end”), of unknown ultimate origin.
Cognate with Saterland Frisian Top (“top”), Cimbrian sòpf (“braid”), Dutch top (“top, summit, peak”), German T

gloss: A person of mixed black and Portuguese descent.
etymology: From Portuguese topaz, of uncertain origin.

gloss: To fall headlong; topple
etymology: From Middle English torplen, of obscure origin. Compare torfel and topple.

gloss: Any of various land-dwelling reptiles, of the family Testudinidae (chiefly Canada, US) or the order Testudines (chiefly UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, South Africa, India), whose body is enclose
etymology: From Middle English tortuse, tortuce, tortuge, from Medieval Latin tortuca, of uncertain origin. gloss: To steal copper, particularly from ship hulls
etymology:
From 19th-century British thieves' cant, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from *tarsh, a metathetic alteration of trash; or from toss.
Sense of nonsense possibly influenced by tush (“nonsense! tsk tsk!”) attested from 15th century.

gloss: A throw, a lob, of a ball etc., with an initial upward direction, particularly with a lack of care.
etymology:
From Middle English tossen (“to buffet about, agitate, toss; to sift or winnow”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse (compare dialectal Norwegian tossa, dialectal Swedish tossa (“to strew, spread”)), or perhaps from an alteration of Middle English tosen (“to tease, pull apart, shred; to wound, injure”). Compare also Dutch tassen (“to pile or heap up, stack”).

gloss: To throw with an initial upward direction.
etymology:
From Middle English tossen (“to buffet about, agitate, toss; to sift or winnow”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse (compare dialectal Norwegian tossa, dialectal Swedish tossa (“to strew, spread”)), or perhaps from an alteration of Middle English tosen (“to tease, pull apart, shred; to wound, injure”). Compare also Dutch tassen (“to pile or heap up, stack”).

gloss: A small child.
etymology:
Borrowed from Scots tot, a shortened form of totum (“small child; tot”), of uncertain origin, perhaps shortened from totter (“to move in an unsteady way”),
Compare tottle, also Old Norse tottr (“name of a dwarf”), Swedish tutte (“small child”), Danish tommeltot (“little child”).

gloss: To continue over time.; To observe the (measured) state of a person or object over time.
etymology: From Middle English trak, tracke, from Old French trac (“track of horses, trail, trace”), of uncertain origin. Likely from a Germanic source, either Old Norse traðk ("a track; path; trodden spot"; > Icelandic traðk (“a track; path; tread”), Faroese traðk (“track; tracks”), Norwegian tråkke (“to trample”)) or from Middle Dutch trec, *trac, treck ("line, row, series"; > Dutch trek (“a draft; feature

gloss: An oblong piece of skin from which the pieces for a glove are cut.
etymology: Attested since the 1860s, of unclear origin. Perhaps from French tranche.

gloss: An ornamental covering or harness for a horse; caparison.
etymology: From Middle English trappyng, trappynge, from trap, trappe (“personal belongings, owndom, household goods”) (compare Middle English trappen (“to deck, caparison”)), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Anglo-Norman, from Medieval Latin trapus (“cloth”), from Frankish *traba, *trapa (“cloth, thread, rag”), from Proto-Germanic *trabō, *trafą, *trēb (“fringe, rags”), from Proto-Indo-European *drāp-, *d

gloss: A braid, knot, or curl, of hair; a ringlet.
etymology: From Middle English tresse, from Old French tresce, of uncertain origin; possibly from Vulgar Latin *trichia, from Ancient Greek τριχία (trikhía, “rope”), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”). Compare French tresse, Italian treccia.

gloss: To braid or knot hair.
etymology: From Middle English tresse, from Old French tresce, of uncertain origin; possibly from Vulgar Latin *trichia, from Ancient Greek τριχία (trikhía, “rope”), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”). Compare French tresse, Italian treccia.

gloss: An English dessert made from a mixture of thick custard, fruit, sponge cake, jelly and whipped cream.
etymology: From Middle English trifle, trifel, triful, trefle, truyfle, trufful, from Old French trufle (“mockery”), a byform of trufe, truffe (“deception”), of uncertain origin.

gloss: To act in a secret, and often dishonest, way; to have secret, and often dishonest, dealings; to intrigue, to scheme.
etymology:
Possibly borrowed from Scots trinket, trincket; further origin unknown, possibly related to:
* trinket (“item used in a religious rite (also, a religious rite, belief, etc.) regarded as superfluous or trivial”) (see etymology 1); or
* trick (noun) or trick (verb).

gloss: An article of clothing that covers the part of the body between the waist and the ankles or knees, and is divided into a separate part for each leg.
etymology:
Attested since the 1610s, from the earlier form trouzes (attested since the 1580s), extended from trouse (1570s), with plural ending typical of things in pairs, from Middle Irish triubus (“close-fitting shorts”), from Old Irish tribus, of uncertain origin. The unexplained intrusive second -r- is perhaps due to the influence of drawers. Doublet of trews (“trousers”).

gloss: A flat-bottomed vessel, of width similar to or greater than its height, used for storing or packing things, or for washing things in.
etymology: From Middle English tubbe, tobbe, from Middle Dutch tubbe or Middle Low German tubbe, tobbe, further etymology unknown. Considered to be unrelated to tube.

gloss: Of a cow: seeking a bull to mate with.
etymology: Origin unknown.

gloss: An underground or underwater passage.
etymology: From Middle French tonnelle (“net”) or tonel (“cask”), diminutive of Old French tonne (“cask”), a word of uncertain origin and affiliation. Related to Old English tunne (“tun; cask; barrel”). More at tun.

gloss: A male sheep, a ram.
etymology: From Middle English tupe (compare Scots tuip), origin unknown.

gloss: To hit, slap.
etymology: Unknown origin. Possibly cognate with Old Norse þveit (“cut, slit, forest clearing”), and if so a doublet of thwaite. May however simply be onomatopoeic or sound-symbolic.

gloss: Intense lovesickness; infatuation, limerence.
etymology: Borrowed from Guyanese Creole English typee; further origin unknown, claimed to be from an Indo-Aryan language but no etymon has been found.

gloss: A usurper; one who gains power and rules extralegally, distinguished from kings elevated by election or succession.
etymology: From Middle English tyraunt, tiraunt, tyrant, tyrante, from Old French tyrant, from the addition of a terminal -t to tiran (cp. French tyran) via a back-formation related to the development of French present participles out of the Latin -ans form, from Latin tyrannus (“despot”), from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “usurper, monarch, despot”), of uncertain origin.

gloss: A selective progesterone receptor modulator used in the acetate form for emergency contraception and to treat uterine fibroids.
etymology: From uli- (of unknown origin) + (mife)prist(one) + a(cety)l.

gloss: The world, a place where difficulties and the sorrows of life are felt, especially (Christianity) as a place to be left behind when one dies and goes to heaven.
etymology: Calque of Latin lacrimārum vallis from the “Salve Regina” (a hymn to the Virgin Mary), based on Hebrew עמק הבכא (ʿēmeq habbāḵāʾ) from Psalm 84:6 of the Bible. The Hebrew term may mean “valley of the baka tree”, a tree of uncertain species (compare 2 Samuel 5:23–24 where baka is used to refer to a tree, and is often translated into English as “balsam tree”, “mulberry tree”, or “poplar tree”), but a

gloss: A drug taken orally in the form of its tartrate C₁₃H₁₃N₃·C₄H₆O₆ as an aid to stop smoking. It binds to nicotinic cell receptors to block the activity of nicotine while also acting as an agonist to red
etymology: From vare- (of unknown origin) + -nicline (“nicotinic cholinergic receptor agonist”).

gloss: A blood vessel that transports blood from the capillaries back to the heart.
etymology: From Middle English veyne, borrowed from Anglo-Norman veine, from Latin vēna (“a blood-vessel; vein; artery”) of uncertain origin. See vēna for more. Doublet of vena. Displaced native edre, from ǣdre (whence edder).

gloss: A drug that functions as an SNRI and is used in the form of its hydrochloride C₁₇H₂₇NO₂·HCl especially to treat depression, anxiety, and panic disorder. It is marketed under the trademark Effexor.
etymology: Probably from venla- (of unknown origin) + ph(enyl) + -ax- (“alteration of (cycloh)exa(ne)”) + (am)ine.

gloss: changeable; protean; having a form, nature or appearance that changes often
etymology: Formed from versi- ‘turning, changing’ (combinatory form of Latin versus ‘turn’) + ultimately Latin pellis ‘skin’. (Used initially as a word of unknown origin in Nathaniel Ward's Discolliminium, or A Most Obedient Reply to a Late Book called 'Bounds and Bonds' By B)

gloss: A medieval poleaxe bearing resemblance to a glaive or a Lochaber ax, although the blade portion is somewhat more elongated.
etymology: From French voulge, vouge, of uncertain origin, but perhaps from or related to Medieval Latin vidubium. (Some references suggest a comparison to Latin vanga instead.)

gloss: Something (such as clouds or smoke) carried aloft by the wind.
etymology:
Origin unknown; possibly related to the following words:
* waff (“waving movement; gust or puff of air or wind; odour, scent; slight blow; slight attack of illness; glimpse; apparition, wraith; of the wind: to cause (something) to move to and fro; to flutter or wave to and fro in the wind; to produce a current of air by waving, to fan”) (Northern England, Scotland), a variant of waive (etymology 2

gloss: A small case, often flat and often made of leather, for keeping money (especially paper money), credit cards, etc.
etymology: From Middle English walet (“a bag, knapsack”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from an assumed Old Northern French *walet (“a roll; bag; a knapsack”), from Proto-Germanic *wal- (“to roll”). More at walk, well, wallow.

gloss: A house or dwelling.
etymology: From Middle English wōne, wāne (“dwelling," "custom”), of unclear origins, compare wont.

gloss: An unkempt and useless person; a loafer.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; possibly a clipping of warble (“the maggot of a warble-fly”).

gloss: To equip with a weapon; to arm.
etymology:
From Middle English wepen, from Old English wǣpn, from Proto-West Germanic *wāpn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną (“weapon”), of unknown origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wēbnom.
Cognates
Cognate with North Frisian woopen (“weapon”), Saterland Frisian Woapen (“weapon”), West Frisian and Dutch wapen (“weapon; coat of arms”), German Waffe (“weapon”) and Wappen (“coat of arms”), Luxembourgish Waf

gloss: A young offspring of a various carnivores (canid, ursid, felid, pinniped), especially of a dog or a wolf, the young of a bear or similar mammal (lion, tiger, seal); a pup, wolf cub.
etymology: From Middle English whelp, from Old English hwelp, from Proto-West Germanic *hwelp, from Proto-Germanic *hwelpaz (compare Dutch welp, German Welpe, Welfe, Old Norse hvelpr, Norwegian Nynorsk kvelp, Danish hvalp), from pre-Germanic *kʷelbos, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A light ship used to navigate inland waterways.
etymology: From Middle English whery (“small boat”), of obscure origin but cognate to French houari and Breton ouari, as well as Welsh chweri (“small boat”).

gloss: To a superlative extent, very, extremely
etymology: From Middle English wicked, wikked, an alteration of Middle English wicke, wikke (“morally perverse, evil, wicked”). Of uncertain origin. Possibly from an adjectival use of Old English wiċċa (“wizard, sorcerer”), from Proto-West Germanic *wikkō (“necromancer, sorcerer”), though the phonology makes this theory difficult to explain. Alternatively, perhaps related to English wicker, Old Norse víkja (

gloss: Eccentric, silly, scatterbrained.
etymology: From *wift + -y. First element is of unknown origin.

gloss: To endeavor to gain someone's affection/support.
etymology: From Middle English wowen, woȝen, from Old English wōgian (“to woo, court, marry”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Scots wow (“to woo”). Perhaps related to Old English wōg, wōh (“bending, crookedness”), in the specific sense of "bend or incline (some)one toward oneself". gloss: The yaffle bird; the European green woodpecker.
etymology: From Middle English wodewale, of uncertain origin, probably from Old English, but perhaps from Middle Dutch wedewale with 1st element reanalyzed as from Middle English wode (“wood”).

gloss: One who guides strangers; a guide or tour guide.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ξεναγωγός (xenagōgós), from ξένος (xénos, “foreigner; guest; stranger”, noun) (possibly ultimately Pre-Greek) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “(adjective) guiding, leading; (noun) escort, guide”) (from ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to bring along, lead”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ- (“to drive”)) + -ός (-ós, suffix forming agentive or patientive adjectives and nouns)). By surf

gloss: A person who breaks open safes; a burglar.
etymology: Origin unknown.

gloss: Expression of shock and alarm.
etymology: Attested from mid-20th century, perhaps derived from yoicks, a hunting call used to urge hounds after a fox, which is attested from 1765–1775, that also is sometimes used as an exclamation of excitement or triumph. gloss: In time long past; long ago.
etymology: From Middle English yore, yoare, yare, ȝore, ȝare, ȝeare, from Old English ġeāra (“long ago”), of unclear origin but probably from Proto-Germanic *jērǫ̂ (literally “of years”), the genitive plural of Proto-Germanic *jērą (“year”). More at year.

gloss: A leukotriene antagonist C₃₁H₃₃N₃O₆S that is administered orally to inhibit bronchoconstriction in the treatment of asthma.
etymology: From zafir- (of unknown origin) + -lukast (“leukotriene receptor antagonist”).

gloss: An antiviral drug C₁₂H₂₀N₄O₇ that is a neuraminidase inhibitor taken by oral inhalation in the treatment and prophylaxis of Influenzavirus.
etymology: From zan- (of unknown origin) + -amivir (“neuraminidase inhibitor”).

gloss: Style, glamor (especially in regard to clothing).
etymology: UK 1960s. Unclear origin; one explanation is that it was borrowed from Angloromani yuser (“clean”, verb) and yusher (“clear”, verb), from Angloromani yus-, yuz-, yuzh- (“clean”) and yush- (“clear”), from Romani žuž-, už- (“clean”, adjective) (also compare Hindi उज्ज्वल (ujjval, “bright”)), but this has been seen as problematic. Another theory is that the term is instead an "expressive formation" s

gloss: A dry red wine of California.
etymology: Unknown origin; wine sense used from 1896, grape sense from 1880. Possibly a transmission of German Zierfandler, a different wine grape, through a Hungarian intermediary such as czirifandli (now Cirfandli).

gloss: A device used for viewing perspective prints, consisting of a lens and a slanting mirror on a stand.
etymology: First part of Unknown origin and meaning, + -scope.

gloss: To hit hard .
etymology: First attested around 1950. Unknown origin, likely imitative, of echoic origin.

gloss: Used to form names of benzodiazepine derivatives used as benzodiazepine receptor antagonists and agonists.
etymology: From (benzodi)aze(pi)n(e) + -il (of unknown origin).

gloss: Used to form names of carboline derivatives used as benzodiazepine receptor antagonists and agonists.
etymology: From car(boli)n(e) + -il (of unknown origin).

gloss: Used to form names of quinoline derivatives used as benzodiazepine receptor full, partial, or inverse agonists.
etymology: From quin(oline) + -il (of unknown origin).

gloss: Used to form names of brominated salicylamide derivatives used as disinfectants.
etymology: From -sal- (“salicylic acid derivative”) + -an (of unknown origin).

gloss: Police or law enforcement, collectively.
etymology:
Of uncertain origin. Widespread use of the phrase as an anti-police slogan grew following the 2014 killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri.
* Possibly from 1312, an alternative form of ACAB (“all cops are bastards”) in which the letters are substituted with their position in the alphabet.
* Alternatively, from the American police procedural television series Adam-12 (1968–1975), in which 1-

gloss: To leave, particularly quickly or at an advantageous time.
etymology: From twenty-three (“get lost; get out; leave”) + skidoo (“to depart, especially quickly”). Exact origin unknown; many theories exist, though none have been universally accepted. See the Wikipedia article for more information.

gloss: The capital city of the province of A Coruña, Galicia, Spain.
etymology: From Galician A Coruña, of uncertain origin.

gloss: The leader of a group of thieves.
etymology: From Latin Aaron, from Ancient Greek Ἀαρών (Aarṓn), from Hebrew אַהֲרֹן (ʾAhărōn), of unknown meaning, possibly meaning “bearer of martyrs”, or perhaps also, or instead, related to the Ancient Egyptian ꜥḥꜣ rw (“warrior lion”), though it has been suggested to also mean “elevated”, “exalted” or “high mountain”. Doublet of Harun.

gloss: A river in the infernal regions; also, the infernal regions themselves. By some of the English poets, it was supposed to be a flaming lake or gulf.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin Acherōn, from Ancient Greek Ἀχέρων (Akhérōn), probably Pre-Greek but folk-etymologically said to be from ἄχος (ákhos, “pain, distress”) + ῥέον (rhéon, “stream”).

gloss: A port city in northern Israel, holiest city in the Baháʼí Faith.
etymology: Borrowed from French and Latin Acre, from Ancient Greek Ἄκο (Áko) or Ἄκη (Ákē), from Hebrew עכו (ʿAkko), of unknown origin.

gloss: A river in South America.
etymology: From Portuguese Acre, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
Various origins:
* Borrowed from Norwegian Aga, a habitational surname of uncertain derivation.
* Borrowed from Turkish Ağa, an occupational surname from ağa (“lord; chief, boss”).
* Borrowed from Amharic አጋ (ʾäga).

gloss: A surname from Hawaiian.
etymology: A Hawaiian surname of unclear origin.

gloss: A surname from Hawaiian.
etymology: From Hawaiian, a surname of unclear origin.

gloss: The third-largest island of the Channel Islands.
etymology: Of obscure origin, see Wikipedia.

gloss: The capital city of Aleppo Governorate, Syria.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian Aleppo, from French Alep, from Ottoman Turkish حلب (haleb), from Arabic حَلَب (ḥalab), of uncertain origin. Theorized to be from Arabic حَلَبَ (ḥalaba, “gave out milk”), coming from the ancient tradition that Abraham gave milk to travelers as they moved throughout the region. Attested in Akkadian as 𒌷𒄩𒆷𒀊𒆠 (ᵁᴿᵁḫa-la-abᴷᴵ, “Ḫalab/Ḫalap”), Hittite 𒄬𒉺 (Ḥalpa), Ugaritic 𐎈𐎍𐎁 (ḥlb),

gloss: A city and port town in the province of Sassari, Sardinia, Italy.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian Alghero, of unclear origin. Usually thought to derive from Medieval Latin Aleguerium (literally “stagnation of seaweed”) or Sardinian S'Alighèra, from aliga (“seaweed; rubbish”) + -era, but either way from Latin alga (“seaweed”), from Proto-Indo-European *alg-, *alǵ- (“to be dirty, slimy”).

gloss: Synonym of American climbing fern (Lygodium palmatum)
etymology: Of unclear origin. Seemingly first mentioned in a letter written in November 1900 and published in January 1901 in Fern Bulletin, in which William R. Maxon describes its sale in Washington, DC, by "old negro women [...among whom] it goes altogether by the name of 'Alice's fern,' a new one, perhaps, to most fern students". In September 1901, her father's rise to the US presidency made Alice Rooseve

gloss: A number of places in England:; A former civil parish (abolished 2024) and adjacent suburb of Bridport, Dorset (OS grid ref SY4693).
etymology:
* Kent, near Lenham: Recorded as Alnoitone in 1086 (DB), Eilnothinton in 1242, from Old English Æþelnōþ (male personal name) + -ing (“belonging to”) + tūn (“homestead”).
* Kent, near Maidstone: Recorded as Elentun in 1086 (DB), from Old English Ælla or Ælle (male personal names) + -ing (“belonging to”) tūn (“homestead”).
* Lincolnshire, and Wiltshire (east of Devizes): Recorded in 1086 (DB) as Ade

gloss: A state of the North Region, Brazil. Capital: Macapá.
etymology: From Portuguese Amapá, of uncertain indigenous origin.

gloss: The ideal stressing egalitarianism and that every citizen of the United States should have an equal opportunity to achieve material prosperity through hard work, determination, and initiative.
etymology: Of unknown origin. First attested in the 1910s. Popularized by American writer and historian James Truslow Adams in 1931.

gloss: The language of this people
etymology: From Biblical Hebrew אֲמֹרִי (ʾĂmōrî) + -ite, of uncertain origin; compare Akkadian 𒈥𒌅 (Amurrum).

gloss: Of or pertaining to this people or language
etymology: From Biblical Hebrew אֲמֹרִי (ʾĂmōrî) + -ite, of uncertain origin; compare Akkadian 𒈥𒌅 (Amurrum).

gloss: Ellipsis of Isle of Arran, Scotland.
etymology:
Derived from Scottish Gaelic Arainn, but the name is ultimately probably of non-Indo-European (substrate) or Pictish origin, along with other uncertain names in Scotland such as Skye, Lewis, and Islay.
Possibly from a Brythonic/Pictish term ancestral or cognate to Middle Welsh aran (“"high place"”).

gloss: A state in northeastern India. Capital: Dispur.
etymology: Of unclear origin, but generally agreed to be related to Ahom. More at Etymology of Assam on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

gloss: The Atlantic Ocean.
etymology: From Middle English Atlantyke, from Latin Ā̆tlanticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτλαντικός (Atlantikós, “Atlantean, of Atlas”), from Ancient Greek Ἄτλᾱς (Átlās), either from ἁ- (ha-, copulative prefix) + Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“bear, undergo, endure”) or of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Pertaining to the Atlantic Ocean.
etymology: From Middle English Atlantyke, from Latin Ā̆tlanticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτλαντικός (Atlantikós, “Atlantean, of Atlas”), from Ancient Greek Ἄτλᾱς (Átlās), either from ἁ- (ha-, copulative prefix) + Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“bear, undergo, endure”) or of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: A steam locomotive of the 4-4-2 wheel arrangement.
etymology: From Middle English Atlantyke, from Latin Ā̆tlanticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτλαντικός (Atlantikós, “Atlantean, of Atlas”), from Ancient Greek Ἄτλᾱς (Átlās), either from ἁ- (ha-, copulative prefix) + Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“bear, undergo, endure”) or of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: A particular model or individual specimen of the Atlas missile and launch vehicle line.
etymology: From Latin Ā̆tlās, from Ancient Greek Ἄτλας (Átlas), either from ἁ- (ha-, copulative prefix) + Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“bear, undergo, endure”) or of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Of or related to Attica, ancient Athens and its hinterland; Synonym of Athenian, of or related to the culture of ancient Athens.
etymology: From Latin Atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós), from some Pre-Greek demonym or toponym for Athens and its hinterland of Attica + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to a modified and clipped Athens + -ic. Doublet of Atticus.

gloss: A king of the tribes of Huns.
etymology:
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀττίλα (Attíla), of uncertain further origin. Traditionally thought to have been derived from East Germanic, such as a Gothic *𐌰𐍄𐍄𐌹𐌻𐌰 (*attila, literally “little father”), from 𐌰𐍄𐍄𐌰 (atta, “father”) + -𐌹𐌻𐌰 (-ila).

gloss: The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed in the Avestan language.
etymology: From Iranian Persian اوستا (avestâ), from Middle Persian [script needed] (ʾp(y)stʾk' /⁠abestāg⁠/), of uncertain meaning.

gloss: Avestan language.
etymology: From Iranian Persian اوستا (avestâ), from Middle Persian [script needed] (ʾp(y)stʾk' /⁠abestāg⁠/), of uncertain meaning.

gloss: A city and municipality, the capital of the province of Badajoz, Extremadura, Spain.
etymology: From Spanish Badajoz, of uncertain origin but possibly from Arabic forms of Latin Pax Augusta.

gloss: A village in Nova Scotia, Canada.
etymology:
Derived from a Mi'kmaq toponym of uncertain origin. The name may derive from Mi'kmaq petek (“turn, bend backwards”).
Compare Bedeque.

gloss: From or characteristic of the Baroque period.
etymology: Via French (which originally meant a pearl of irregular shape) from Portuguese barroco (“irregular pearl”); related to Spanish barrueco and Italian barocco and Sicilian baroccu, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly from Latin verruca (“wart”), or possibly from the technical construction of scholastic logic, Baroco.

gloss: Any of a number of places:; A coastal town and community with a town council in Vale of Glamorgan borough county borough, Wales (OS grid ref ST1167).
etymology: In Wales, said to be named after Saint Baruc, who was buried on Barry Island, from Welsh Barrwg, a name of uncertain origin but possibly related to Irish barr (“hill, summit”).

gloss: A wicked demon in Christian and Jewish apocrypha.
etymology:
Latin Bĕlĭal, Hebrew בְלִיַּעַל.
Of uncertain origin. It has been conventionally been interpreted as בְּלִי (“without”) + a word meaning "use" (hence "useless, worthless"), but it is unclear what the latter word is.

gloss: A placename; A federal city of Switzerland; the capital city of Bern canton.
etymology:
From Alemannic German Bärn, of uncertain further origin.
A popular folk etymology says it was named by its founder, Berthold V, Duke of Zähringen, after the first animal he saw in the area, a Bär(in) (“bear”) (compare Berlin, subject to a similar folk etymology).

gloss: A town in Assam.
etymology: Of unclear origin, but it has an etymological connection to the Assamese word Bhuri, which means rice husk.

gloss: A Barbadian.
etymology: From the 1860s. Origin unknown. Perhaps from Igbo bem (“my home, household, folk, fellows”).

gloss: A nickname for Barbados.
etymology: From the 1860s. Origin unknown. Perhaps from Igbo bem (“my home, household, folk, fellows”).

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
Various origins:
* Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Beolláin (“descendant of Beollán”), a personal name of uncertain origin.
* A variant of Bowland, an English habitational surname.
* Borrowed from German Boland, a surname of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
Various origins:
* Borrowed from Assamese বৰা (bora), a surname of unclear origin.
* Borrowed from Romanian Bora, a feminine hypocoristic form of the personal name Boris.
* Borrowed from Polish Bora, a pet form of Borzyslaw or Bolebor.
* Borrowed from Hungarian Bora, a variant of Bara.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: The town in Ireland is from Irish Bré, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname from Italian.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian Bria, a surname of uncertain meaning.

gloss: A surname from Scottish Gaelic.
A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Ó Bróithe (“descendant of Bróth”), a personal name or byname of unknown origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
* As an English surname, from the noun brow.
* As a French surname, variant of Brault and also Breaux. Compare Bro, Broe.
* As a Dutch surname, Americanized from Brouw, either from the verb brouwen (“to brew”) or a variant of op den Brouw, a toponym of uncertain origin (possibly itself related to brouwen).

gloss: A surname from Old English.
etymology: From Old English Budda, a nickname of uncertain meaning.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. It may be a variant of Beadling.

gloss: A comune in Caserta, Italy.
etymology:
From Italian Caiazzo, possibly from an unattested intermediate form Vulgar Latin *Caiatium, ultimately from Latin Caiatia, under possible influence from Italian -azzo (“forming pejoratives and diminutives”), of uncertain origin. gloss: A historical county in the far north of Scotland, which was abolished and merged into Highland Region in 1975, which became the Highland council area in 1996.
etymology: The placename is of Pictish origin, named after a tribe called the Catti, with the common Old Norse suffix -ness (“headland”). The tribe name is of uncertain origin, but compare *katus (“battle”).

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Callanáin (“descendant of Callanán”), a personal name of unclear origin.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Ó Cearmada (“descendant of Cearmaid”), a personal name of unknown origin.

gloss: A city and prefecture, the capital of Savoie department, Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, France.
etymology: From French Chamberi, from Medieval Latin Chamberium << Cambariaco << Cambariacum << Camefriacum, of uncertain origin, possibly Gaulish *camboritos (“bent ford”); see Breton Kemper. More at Chambéry.

gloss: A Circassian.
etymology: From Russian черке́с (čerkés), of disputed origin, with suggestions including Turkic or Mongolic. See Circassians.

gloss: Alternative letter-case form of china: porcelain tableware.
etymology: From Portuguese China, from possibly Venetan Cina probably under influence from Old French Chin, from Classical Persian چین (čīn) under influence from Medieval Latin Sina (“China”), from Middle Persian 𐭰𐭩𐭭 (Čīn, “China”), from Sanskrit चीन (cīna, “the Chinese; China”) of uncertain etymology. It is usually thought to be derived from Chinese 秦 (Qín) (sm Qín, mc d͡ziɪn, oc *zin, "Qin"), the westernmo

gloss: A chayote.
etymology: First attested in 1886, but of uncertain origin (present Chinese terms for the breed do not resemble it). Possibly related to the old Chinese custom of eating dogs (cf. chow and chow-chow).

gloss: A town in Clackmannanshire council area, Scotland, which was the county town of the historic county of Clackmannanshire until 1822 (OS grid ref NS9192).
etymology: Derived from Scottish Gaelic siorrachd chlach Mhannainn (“county with the stone of Manau”). For the second element see cloch (“stone”). The last element is from Celtic, but of unknown meaning; see Manau.

gloss: A large village and civil parish in Bolsover district, Derbyshire, England (OS grid ref SK4975).
etymology: From Old Welsh *Colün (“water, river”), from Proto-Brythonic *Colaunā, of unknown meaning.

gloss: A major river in Scotland, flowing from South Lanarkshire council area, past North Lanarkshire council area, through Glasgow council area, and past Renfrewshire council area and West Dunbartonshire co
etymology: The name of a river in Scotland, from the Gaelic name Cluaidh, of uncertain origin. Possibly influenced by clut (“the cleansing one”).

gloss: A land of plenty, luxury and idleness.
etymology:
From Old French cocagne, of obscure origin, but the many references to sweet delicacies in the 13th century poem that is the first record of the word suggest it may have come from a Germanic word for a cake, probably the ancestor of the modern German Kuchen.
See also Proto-Germanic *kōkô.
May also relate to or be influenced by Old Irish cucainn (“food ration, sweet pie”).

gloss: From the East End of London, or London generally.
etymology: First attested in Samuel Rowland's 1600 The Letting of Humours Blood in the Head-Vaine as "a Bowe-bell Cockney", from Middle English cokenay (“a spoiled child; a milksop, an effeminate man”), used in the 16th c. by English country folk as a term of disparagement for city dwellers, of uncertain etymology. Possibly from Middle English cokeney (“a small, misshapen egg”), from coken (“cocks'(rooster’s

gloss: Synonym of La Coruña.
etymology: From Spanish La Coruña, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A cathedral city and metropolitan borough of the West Midlands, in central England, historically in Warwickshire.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English Coventre, from Old English Cofentrēo, Cofantrēo, of obscure origin. Believed to be derived from an Anglo-Saxon named Cofa, hence Cofantrēo (literally “Cofa's tree”).

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
Uncertain origin and variable origins depending on the ancestry of the bearer :
* In some cases, possibly borrowed from Sicilian crapu (“he-goat”), masculine and obsolete form of crapa (“she-goat”). Compare also Italian capro.
* In some cases, from French Crépeau, derived from Middle French Crespeau or Crepeau, itself from Old French cresp.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Críodáin (“descendant of Críodán”), a personal name of obscure origin.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Ó Colla (“descendant of Colla”), a personal name of unknown origin.

gloss: A Thessalian princess and huntress demigod, companion of Artemis and lover of Apollo.
etymology: From Latin Cyrene, from Ancient Greek Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē), of uncertain origin. Classical sources considered the Thessalian demigod the etymon for the Libyan city. Modern scholars variously derive the name from the Libyan spring Κύρα (Kúra) or, noting the myth attested before the spring or city, consider an existing Proto-Berber name to have been conflated with the Thessalian myths by early Greek colo

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Déiseach, a name for a member of a vassal community called Déise, a word of uncertain meaning and origin.

gloss: An American surname.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Dawnay, or else an altered form of Dan or Daniel.

gloss: The variety of the Persian language that is chiefly used in Afghanistan, contrasted with varieties spoken elsewhere such as Iranian Persian or Tajik.
etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian دری (darī), of disputed origin, probably from دربار (darbār, “royal court”). The term was adopted by the government of Afghanistan in 1964 as the official name of the varieties of Persian spoken in the country, which has become the most common usage of the term since.

gloss: A river in South Yorkshire, England, which flows into the River Don.
etymology: From Middle English Dern, Dyrne, Dirne, Dirna, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old English dierne (“hidden, concealed”), or of Celtic origin.

gloss: A megacity and union territory of India, containing the national capital New Delhi.
etymology: Corrupted from Hindustani دہلی (dihlī, dêhli) / देहली (dehlī), of uncertain origin. See Delhi § Toponym at Wikipedia. Compare Hindi दिल्ली (dillī).

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology:
Two main origins:
* Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Duibheannaigh (“descendant of Duibheannach”), a personal name of unclear origin, but perhaps composed of the elements dubh (“black”) and eanach (“marshy place”).
* Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Duibheamhna (“descendant of Dubheamhna”), a personal name composed of the elements dubh (“black”) and the genitive form of Eamhain (“Navan Fort, t

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
Two possible origins:
* Borrowed from German Dröge, a nickname of uncertain derivation.
* Borrowed from Dutch Droge, a nickname from Middle Dutch drôge (“dry, boring, unfriendly”).

gloss: A market town and metropolitan borough of the West Midlands, England.
etymology: From Old English, literally "wood or clearing of Dudda (a personal name of unknown meaning)".

gloss: A city and former royal burgh of Fife council area, Scotland (OS grid ref NT0987); The former capital of Scotland.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic Dùn Phàrlain, the first element being from dùn (“fortification”), and the rest of uncertain origin, possibly from an alteration of the river Lyne Burn, from linne (“waterfall, pool”) + bùrn (“water”).

gloss: A state of Mexico.
etymology: Named after the city of Durango, in northern Spain, of uncertain origin, probably from Basque Duranco, but possibly from Basque Urazango, Basque Padurango, or a Roman fundus, Late Latin Turanicus. More at Durango on Wikipedia.

gloss: A surname from Polish.
etymology: From a Slavic language, e.g. Polish Dybał, from dybać, from Proto-Slavic *dybati, of uncertain origin.

gloss: The capital city of Scotland.
etymology: From Middle English Edynburgh, from Cumbric Eidyn, a Celtic/Brythonic region of uncertain origin (possibly a personal name; compare Proto-Celtic *dūnom (“stronghold”)) + Old English burg (“castle, stronghold”). The English name was probably a calque from Cumbric (cf. Din Eidyn). More at Eidyn and Etymology of Edinburgh.

gloss: A village and civil parish in Guildford borough, Surrey, England (OS grid ref TQ1253).
etymology: From Old English, "Effa's farmstead," from *Effa + -ing + ham (“home”). The first element is a variant of Æffa, Uffa, a king of the Angles (c. 575), attested in names such as Abridge, Uffington, and Ufford, but of uncertain origin.

gloss: A cathedral city and civil parish (served by City of Ely Council) in East Cambridgeshire district, Cambridgeshire, England.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English Ely, from Old English Ēlīġ, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A river in West Asia, 2780 kilometers in length, flowing southwest from Turkey, then southeast, and uniting with the Tigris before entering the Persian Gulf. It forms the Western edge of classical Mes
etymology: From Latin Euphrātēs, from Ancient Greek Εὐφράτης (Euphrátēs), from Old Persian 𐎢𐎳𐎼𐎠𐎬𐎢 (u-f-r-a-tu-u /⁠ʰUfrātuš⁠/), from Akkadian 𒀀𒇉𒌓𒄒𒉣 (^(ÍD)Purattu), from Sumerian 𒀀𒇉𒌓𒄒𒉣 (^(ÍD)Buranun) (compare Elamite 𒌑𒅁𒊏𒌅𒅖 (ú-ip-ra-du-iš), Classical Syriac ܦܪܬ (P(ə)rāṯ)). gloss: A market town and civil parish with a town council in Swale borough, Kent, England (OS grid ref TR0161).
etymology: From Old English Fefreshām, of which the second element is hām (“homestead”) and the first element is of uncertain origin; it may come from Latin faber (“smith, craftsman”).

gloss: A surname.
etymology: From Spanish Galván, ultimately from Latin Galbanus, from Galba + -anus (“-an”), from galba (“larva, worm, fatty”), from Gaulish of uncertain meaning. Doublet of Galvao, Galvano, and Galvani.

gloss: A surname from Italian.
etymology: From Italian Galvani, from Galvano + -i (“forming surnames”), from galba (“larva, worm, fatty”), from Gaulish of uncertain meaning. Doublet of Galvano, Galvan, and Galvao.

gloss: A surname from Italian
etymology: From Italian Galvano, from Latin Galbanus, from Galba + -anus (“-an”), from galba (“larva, worm, fatty”), from Gaulish of uncertain meaning. Doublet of Galvao, Galvan, and Galvani.

gloss: A surname from Portuguese.
etymology: From Portuguese Galvão, ultimately from Latin Galbanus, from Galba + -anus (“-an”), from galba (“larva, worm, fatty”), from Gaulish of uncertain meaning. Doublet of Galvan, Galvano, and Galvani.

gloss: A county in the West of the Republic of Ireland.
etymology: Anglicization of Irish Gaillimh, of uncertain meaning, said to mean "stony' (referring to the River Corrib). If so, it probably derives from Old Irish calad (“hard”); compare caillou, of Gaulish origin.

gloss: Ellipsis of Galway hooker.
etymology: Anglicization of Irish Gaillimh, of uncertain meaning, said to mean "stony' (referring to the River Corrib). If so, it probably derives from Old Irish calad (“hard”); compare caillou, of Gaulish origin.

gloss: A town in Newfoundland, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada.
etymology: Etymology unknown.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname from Catalan.
etymology: Borrowed from Catalan Gelpí, of uncertain origin, but compare gelpa (“goblet, cup”), presumably a borrowing from Old French gobelet.

gloss: Of or relating to the nation of Germany.
etymology:
From Latin Germānus, Germānī (“the peoples of Germānia”), as distinct from Gauls (in the writings of Caesar and Tacitus), and of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly Celtic/Gaulish).
Not related to german (“closely related”) or germane (from the Latin adjective germānus, through Old French).
Attested since at least 1520. Replaced the older terms Almain and Dutch (from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz) in

gloss: A municipality of Seville, Andalusia, Spain.
etymology:
* As a Catalan surname, from the saints' name Ginés. Compare Jines.
* The city in Spain is of unclear origin, but could possibly be a corruption of the source of the saints' name above with an Arabic influence, namely جنة (“garden, paradise”), referring to the Garden of Eden.

gloss: A state of the Center-West Region, Brazil, around the city. Capital: Goiânia.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Portuguese Goiás, from earlier Goyaz of uncertain origin but possibly an Old Tupi endonym.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Jewish Ashkenazi surname of unclear origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Scottish surname of uncertain origin.

gloss: Of or relating to Greece, its people, its language, or its culture.
etymology:
Inherited from Old English Grēcas (“Greeks”), variant of Crēcas, from Proto-West Germanic *Krēkō, from Latin Graecus of uncertain origin, perhaps derived from the toponym Γραῖα (Graîa) or from other Paleo-Balkanic forms from a tribal name Graii.
Greek in any case has the cognate Γραικός (Graikós), the mythological ancestor of the Γραίοι (Graíoi, “Graecians”). Germanic cognates include Dutch Griek,

gloss: The language spoken by people of Greece, particularly, depending on context, Ancient Greek or Modern Greek.
etymology:
Inherited from Old English Grēcas (“Greeks”), variant of Crēcas, from Proto-West Germanic *Krēkō, from Latin Graecus of uncertain origin, perhaps derived from the toponym Γραῖα (Graîa) or from other Paleo-Balkanic forms from a tribal name Graii.
Greek in any case has the cognate Γραικός (Graikós), the mythological ancestor of the Γραίοι (Graíoi, “Graecians”). Germanic cognates include Dutch Griek,

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

gloss: A creole of English and various African languages spoken on a group of islands off the coast of the Carolinas and Georgia in the Southern United States.
etymology:
First attested in 1739 as a male black slave's proper name, of unclear origin. Traditionally linked by folk etymology to an apheresis of Angola (where many African slaves were carried from), or an apparent West African ethno-tribal group called the Gola people.
See more at the Wikipedia article Gullah, including other theories.

gloss: A member of the Gullah culture.
etymology:
First attested in 1739 as a male black slave's proper name, of unclear origin. Traditionally linked by folk etymology to an apheresis of Angola (where many African slaves were carried from), or an apparent West African ethno-tribal group called the Gola people.
See more at the Wikipedia article Gullah, including other theories.

gloss: Pertaining to the Gullah language and culture.
etymology:
First attested in 1739 as a male black slave's proper name, of unclear origin. Traditionally linked by folk etymology to an apheresis of Angola (where many African slaves were carried from), or an apparent West African ethno-tribal group called the Gola people.
See more at the Wikipedia article Gullah, including other theories.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology:
Two main origins:
* Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó hAilche (“descendant of Ailche”), a personal name of unclear origin.
* Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó hÁille (“descendant of Áille”), a byname from áille (“beauty”).

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó hAnnáin (“descendant of Annán”), a personal name of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
* As an English surname, variant of Askin.
* Also as an English surname, from Haskayne in Halsall, of Brythonic origin, from hesg (“sedge”) + the suffix -en. Sometimes confused with Heskin and Axon.
* Also as an English surname, variant of Hoskin.
* As an Irish surname, from Ó hUiscin, a name of uncertain origin. Sometimes calqued as Waters due to its similarity to the noun uisce (“water”). Compar

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó hÁbhartaigh (“descendant of Ábhartach”), a personal name of unclear origin.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó hÉighnigh (“descendant of Éighneach”), or an Anglicized form of Ó hÉanna (“descendant of Éanna”), a personal name of unclear origin, possibly containing the element éan (“bird”). Compare Bird, Heagney.

gloss: The islands off the west coast of Scotland, divided into the Inner Hebrides and the Outer Hebrides.
etymology: From Latin Hebudes or Haebudes, with u likely turned to ri by scribal error. Earlier origin unknown, though Venneman (1999) speculatively offers a Proto-Semitic solution in *’y (“island”) + *p d (“lamb”). Compare Ancient Greek Ἕβουδαι (Héboudai), islands mentioned by Ptolemy and Pliny, likely the Hebrides.

gloss: A strait in East River, New York City, New York State, United States; the narrowest part of the East River, separating Manhattan and Long Island.
etymology:
hell+gate
* (New York City): Anglicization of the original Dutch name Dutch Hellegat, of uncertain meaning.

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
* As an English, Scottish, and Swedish surname, from the Old Norse personal name Hemingr, variant of Hæmingr, itself of uncertain origin, possibly from hamr, hemingr (“form, shape; skin of an animal”). This word may have been borrowed into Old English as hemming (“a rawhide boot”).
* As a German surname, variant of Hemme.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Ó hEidhneacháin (“descendant of Eidhneachán”), a personal name of uncertain origin.

gloss: The largest town on the island of Hawaii, in Hawaii County, Hawaii, located at the eastern corner of the island.
etymology: From Hawaiian Hilo, of uncertain etymology but possibly related to hilo (“to twist”).

gloss: Expressing scornful rejection or disbelief.
etymology: UK early 19th century. Etymology unknown.

gloss: A town in the city of Brighton and Hove, on the south coast of East Sussex, England, west of Brighton (OS grid ref TQ2804).
etymology: Of disputed origin, with suggestions including hufe (“covering, shelter”) and hof (“hall”). More at Hove.

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
Two main origins:
* A pet form of the medieval personal name Hudde.
* Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó hUada (“descendant of Uada”), a personal name of uncertain origin.

gloss: A member of the Protestant Reformed Church of France during the 16th and 17th century.
etymology: From French huguenot (“Huguenot”), of uncertain origin.

gloss: Of, like or relating to Huguenotism or Huguenots.
etymology: From French huguenot (“Huguenot”), of uncertain origin.

gloss: A city in Romania.
etymology: From Romanian Iași of uncertain origin.

gloss: The southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides in Argyll and Bute council area, Scotland.
etymology: Derived from Scottish Gaelic Ìle, but probably ultimately of non-Indo-European (substrate) origin, along with other uncertain names in Scotland such as Skye, Lewis, and Arran. The silent s in this word, as in island, is due to an unetymological association with isle.

gloss: The queen of the gods, the equivalent of the Greek goddess Hera.
etymology: From Middle English Juno, from Latin Iūnō of uncertain origin. One hypothesis is derivation from Proto-Indo-European *dyúh₃onh₂- (“she of heavenly authority”), from *dyew- (“sky, heaven”) + *-Hō (“burden, authority”), reflecting her role as goddess of rulers. gloss: The capital and largest city of Afghanistan.
etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian کَابُل (kābul), of unknown origin. See the Persian entry for more.

gloss: A member of a diverse ethnic group originating in Myanmar and Thailand.
etymology: From Burmese ကရင် (ka.rang), of disputed origin.

gloss: A group of Sino-Tibetan languages spoken by people of the Karen ethnic group, also called Karenic.
etymology: From Burmese ကရင် (ka.rang), of disputed origin.

gloss: Alternative form of Kaskian (“ancient Anatolian people”).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Hittite, of uncertain origin. Possibly related to the name of Circassia.

gloss: A port city in northern Greece.
etymology: Borrowed from Greek Καβάλα (Kavála), from Byzantine Greek Καβάλα (Kabála) of uncertain origin.

gloss: A town in Newfoundland, Newfoundland and Labrador.
etymology: Etymology unknown. Proposed etymologies include a corruption of the surname Keough, a derivation from the surname Keel, or a derivation from keel, referring here to the shape of the rocks near the town's harbour.

gloss: Synonym of Karbala, a city in Iraq.
etymology: From Ottoman Turkish كربلا, from Arabic كَرْبَلَاء (Karbalāʔ) of uncertain origin.

gloss: A town in Newfoundland, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada.
etymology: Etymology unknown. Proposed etymologies include a derivation from an archaic dialectal term meaning "bundle of hides" or an English surname.

gloss: A New Yorker, particularly a scion of its old Dutch families
etymology: From Diedrich Knickerbocker, the pseudonym adopted by Washington Irving for his 1809 A History of New York, probably for the Knickerbackers of Schaghticoke, New York, descended from the Dutch immigrant Harmen Jansen van Bommel(l), who went variously by the names van Wy(y)e, van Wyekycback(e), Kinnekerbacker, Knickelbacker, Knickerbacker, Kinckerbacker, Nyckbacker, and Kynckbacker. The surname is o

gloss: A volcano on Hawaii Island.
etymology: From Hawaiian Kohala, of uncertain meaning. Sometimes mistakenly derived from kohola (“whale”), which are plentiful in the area.

gloss: A city in Kerala, in southwestern India.
etymology:
From Malayalam കോഴിക്കോട് (kōḻikkōṭŭ). The name probably corresponds to Ancient Greek Καλαικαρίας (Kalaikarías), mentioned by Ptolemy, of uncertain meaning. The second element is likely Sanskrit कोट (koṭa, “fortress, palace”). The first element could be from Kali, wife of Shiva, meaning "palace of Kali," or it could instead be a Dravidian name கல்லியை (kalliyai).
The anglicized variant of the name

gloss: Synonym of A Coruña:; A province of Galicia, Spain.
etymology: From Spanish La Coruña, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Scottish surname of unclear origin.

gloss: A hilly area in southwestern Piedmont, Italy.
etymology: From Italian Langhe, plural of Piedmontese langa (“hill”), of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Lideadha (“descendant of Lideadh”), a personal name of unclear origin.

gloss: Synonym of Nicosia, the capital city of Cyprus and Northern Cyprus.
etymology: From Greek Λευκωσία (Lefkosía), from a variant of Byzantine Greek Λευκουσία (Leukousía), equivalent to λευκός (leukós, “white”) or λεύκη (leúkē, “poplar”) + οὐσία (ousía, “property, estate”), but deriving from various Ancient Greek forms including Λευτεῶν (Leuteôn), Λευκοθέον (Leukothéon), and Λευκούπολις (Leukoúpolis) adapting an early or pre-Greek name variously recorded as Λέδραι (Lédrai), Λῆδρ

gloss: The Lesser Key of Solomon, a notable grimoire compiled in the mid-17th century.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin Lemegeton, of unknown further origin and meaning.

gloss: A surname from Hebrew.
etymology: From Russian Левин (Levin), from Леви (Levi) + -ин (-in, “forming possessives & adjectives”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (“Levi”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Levine.

gloss: A surname from Hebrew.
etymology: Borrowed from French Levine, from Russian Левин (Levin), from Леви (Levi) + -ин (-in, “forming possessives & adjectives”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (“Levi”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Levin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: From Middle English Lewes, from late Old English Lewes, a variant of earlier Lǣwe, of uncertain origin. Traditionally derived from Old English hlǣw (“hill”), referring to the several mounts in Lewes. Alternatively, perhaps derived from Old English lǣw (“cut, incision, gash”), referring to the narrow, steep-sided 'gash' where the River Ouse cuts through the line of the South Downs.

gloss: A surname from Polish.
etymology: From Polish Lewi, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (Leví), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Levi.

gloss: Ellipsis of the Isle of Lewis: an island of Scotland, United Kingdom.
etymology: Derived from Scottish Gaelic Leòdhas, of uncertain origin; traditionally referred to Old Norse Ljóðahús, from ljóð (“song, poem”) + hús (“house”); but may be related to the Pictish name of the island recorded in Ptolemy's Geography as Λίμνου (Límnou).

gloss: The capital city of La Rioja, in northern Spain, on the river Ebro.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish Logroño, of unknown origin, but most likely from Old Spanish lo (definite article) + Celtiberian gronio (“ford”).

gloss: A canton of Switzerland.
etymology: From French Lucerne, known in Swiss German as Lozärn, from Medieval Latin Lucernense, Luciaria, Lucerna, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Latin lūcĭus (“pike”) with the suffix -ārĭa, as in "place with a large number of pike." Popular etymology associated it with lucerna (“lantern”), though both words are related to lux (“light”). Also compare Leodegar, Burgundian bishop of Autun.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Loideáin (“descendant of Loideán”), a personal name of obscure origin.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Mac Cába (“son of Cába”), a personal name of uncertain origin.

gloss: A river in Maine-et-Loire department, Pays de la Loire, France, a tributary of the Loire, flowing 12 km through the city of Angers from the confluence of the Mayenne and Sarthe into the Loire.
etymology: From French Maine, from earlier Maienne, from Latin Meduāna, of uncertain origin. Doublet of Mayenne. Unrelated to the French province of the same name.

gloss: A port city, the capital of the province of Malaga, Andalusia, Spain.
etymology: From Spanish Málaga, from Arabic مَالَقَة (Mālaqa), from Latin Malaca, from Phoenician 𐤌𐤋𐤊 (Málaka or Malake) of uncertain origin but possibly derived from Proto-West Semitic *milḥ- (“salt”). The American places are from the Spanish city. The surname is also sometimes derived via Polish Malaga.

gloss: An independent city in Metro Manila, Philippines.
etymology: From Tagalog Mandaluyong, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Maine (“descendant of Maine”), a personal name of obscure origin.

gloss: A city in Pinal County, Arizona, United States.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish, of uncertain origin.

gloss: 5th-century Iranian social reformer and religious activist.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Mac Cearbhaill (“son of Cearbhall”), a personal name of uncertain origin. Compare McCarville, which shares the same etymology

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Mac Cearbhaill (“son of Cearbhall”), a personal name of uncertain origin. Compare McCarroll, which shares the same etymology

gloss: A surname from Scottish Gaelic [in turn from Old Norse].
etymology:
Two main origins:
* Anglicized form of Irish and Scottish Gaelic Mac Amhalghaidh (“son of Amhalghadh”), a personal name of uncertain origin.
* Anglicized form of Irish and Scottish Gaelic Mac Amhlaoibh (“son of Amhlaoibh”), a Gaelicized form of Old Norse Óláfr (“Olaf”).

gloss: A surname from Scottish Gaelic.
etymology: Anglicized form of Scottish Gaelic Mac Gille Iomchadha (“son of the servant of (Saint) Imchad”), a personal name of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish and Scottish Gaelic Mac Colla, a personal name of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Mac Comhdhain (“son of Comhdhan”), a personal name of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: From the Irish and Scottish Gaelic surname, Anglicized form of Mac Neachtain, a patronymic surname from the personal name Neachtan, a name of the god of water in Irish mythology, of uncertain ultimate origin; see Nechtan. Compare McCracken.

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
* As an Irish and Scottish Gaelic surname, Anglicized form of Mac Nuadhat (“son of Nuadha”), the name of ancient Celtic god whose whose name is of unclear origin; see Núadu.
* Also as a Scottish surname, variant of McNaughton.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology:
* As an Irish and Scottish surname, Anglicized form of Northern Irish Mac Péice (“son of Péic”), of non-Celtic but obscure origin, perhaps in actuality related to English peak or its source.
* As an English surname, from Old English pik (see Pike) though it could also be from or influenced by Peak.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Mac Cuaig, a surname of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname from Scottish Gaelic.
etymology: Scottish surname of uncertain origin.

gloss: A province of Saudi Arabia.
etymology: From Arabic مَكَّة (Makka) of uncertain etymology. In American place names, in reference to the Arabian city.

gloss: The city of Milan in the era of Ancient Rome.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin Mediolānum, of uncertain Gaulish origin. Doublet of Milan.

gloss: Pertaining to a Native American people living in the region of Moskitia in Central America.
etymology: From Spanish Mosquito, and its source, Miskito Miskito, of unknown origin.

gloss: A member of these people; a Miskito Indian.
etymology: From Spanish Mosquito, and its source, Miskito Miskito, of unknown origin.

gloss: The Miskito language.
etymology: From Spanish Mosquito, and its source, Miskito Miskito, of unknown origin.

gloss: An island of Croatia.
etymology: From Serbo-Croatian Mljet, from Proto-Slavic *Mьlětъ, from Latin Melita, from Ancient Greek Μελῐ́τη (Melĭ́tē) of uncertain origin. Doublet of Malta and Meleda.

gloss: The fifth largest island of Hawaii.
etymology: From Hawaiian Molokaʻi, of uncertain meaning.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: From the Irish surname of unclear origin.

gloss: A surname from Norwegian, Korean, or Khmer.
etymology:
Various origins:
* Borrowed from Norwegian Mong, a habitational surname from a place in Rogaland.
* Borrowed from Korean 몽 (mong), a surname of unclear origin.
* Borrowed from Khmer ម៉ុង (mong).

gloss: A surname.
etymology:
* As a French surname, variant of Mayrant, itself possibly a variant of Mayrand, from Mayran in Aveyron (Occitan Mairanh), of uncertain origin, possibly Gallo-Roman/Medieval Latin Marianum or Marinus.
* As an English/Norman/French surname, from the Old French personal name Morant, from a Medieval Latin personal name such as Moderandus (“he who is able”) or from Maurandus, based on Maurus (“Moor”).

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Maolaithche (“descendant of the servant of Aithche”), a personal name of unclear origin.

gloss: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–1821), a French military commander and political leader.
etymology: From French Napoléon, from Italian Napoleone, name of an early saint, of uncertain origin; possibly from the Germanic clan name Nibelung. By folk etymology explained as Napoli (“Naples”) + leone (“lion”).

gloss: Alternative form of napoleon.
etymology: From French Napoléon, from Italian Napoleone, name of an early saint, of uncertain origin; possibly from the Germanic clan name Nibelung. By folk etymology explained as Napoli (“Naples”) + leone (“lion”).

gloss: A city in northern Israel.
etymology: Via Latin Nāzareth and Koine Greek Νᾱζᾰρέθ (Nāzăréth) from Hebrew נָצְרַת (nāṣraṯ), of uncertain origin.

gloss: The capital city of Cyprus and Northern Cyprus.

gloss: The westernmost and smallest of the inhabited islands of Hawaii.
etymology: From Hawaiian Niʻihau, of uncertain meaning.

gloss: Alternative letter-case form of nina (“a hidden message revealed in the completed grid of a crossword”).

Borrowed into English in the nineteenth century, apparently from several sources. Many borrowings are of Russian Ни́на (Nína), the name of a Georgian saint in the fourth century, also known as Nino, of obscure origin and meaning, possibly connected with the Assyrian king Ninus. Others are of an Italian short form of diminutives like Annina from Anna and Giovannina from Giovanna.

gloss: The capital of ancient Assyria, now Mosul, Iraq.

gloss: A surname from Irish.
etymology: Anglicized form of Irish Ó hUrthuile (“descendant of Urthuile”), a personal name of obscure origin. Compare Hurley.

gloss: A member of a native Algonquin people of central Canada.
etymology: First attested in English around 1700 (and attested in early French as Outchibouec), from the Ojibwe name of an individual band of Ojibwe, of unclear origin. The most widely accepted theory connects it to Ojibwe ojibwaakide (“it shrivels, it puckers in the fire”), in reference to the puckering or tightening of moccasins at their seams or near fire. gloss: Of or pertaining to this people, culture or language.
etymology: First attested in English around 1700 (and attested in early French as Outchibouec), from the Ojibwe name of an individual band of Ojibwe, of unclear origin. The most widely accepted theory connects it to Ojibwe ojibwaakide (“it shrivels, it puckers in the fire”), in reference to the puckering or tightening of moccasins at their seams or near fire. Alternatively, Helen Tanner and Edmund Danzinger

etymology: From Late Middle English Olympyan, from Latin Olympius (“of or relating to Mount Olympus”) and its etymon Ancient Greek Ὀλῠ́μπῐος (Olŭ́mpĭos, “of or relating to Mount Olympus; living on Mount Olympus; Olympian”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, or forming agent nouns). gloss: Othniel, the first of the biblical judges.
etymology: From Biblical Hebrew עָתְנִיאֵל (ʿOṯnīʾēl), of uncertain meaning but at any rate ending in אֵל (ʾēl, “God”).

gloss: A country in Central America. Official name: Republic of Panama.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish Panamá, of unknown origin. Possibly from a Chibchan language such as Kuna, or another indigenous language of the region (such as Cueva, which is barely attested and is now extinct).

gloss: A Panama hat.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish Panamá, of unknown origin. Possibly from a Chibchan language such as Kuna, or another indigenous language of the region (such as Cueva, which is barely attested and is now extinct).

gloss: A surname.
etymology: Habitational, perhaps from Pinkhurst in Slinfold or Pinkhurst Farm in Abinger, from Old English pinca (“finch”) or a personal name derived from it + hyrst (“hillock copse”). Alternatively perhaps from Pankhurst (Surrey), of obscure origin.

gloss: A country in Oceania. Official name: Independent State of Papua New Guinea. Capital and largest city: Port Moresby.
etymology: From a combination of Papua (of uncertain etymology; see the term for more) and New Guinea, formerly referring to separately-administered dependent territories of Australia.

gloss: An independent city in Metro Manila, Philippines.
etymology: From Spanish Parañaque, from earlier Palañac, an earlier Hispanized form of Tagalog Palanyag, attested in 1582, of uncertain origin.

gloss: A surname.
etymology: English and German surname of uncertain origin; perhaps from a nickname related to Peter.

gloss: An inhabitant of pre-Hellenic Greece.
etymology: From Ancient Greek Πελασγός (Pelasgós) + -ian, presumably based on a Pre-Greek ethnonym. Compare Egyptian pwrꜣsꜣtj, an ethnonym listed as one of the Sea Peoples attacking Egypt around 1190 BCE.

gloss: The language spoken by the Pelasgians.
etymology: From Ancient Greek Πελασγός (Pelasgós) + -ian, presumably based on a Pre-Greek ethnonym. Compare Egyptian pwrꜣsꜣtj, an ethnonym listed as one of the Sea Peoples attacking Egypt around 1190 BCE.

gloss: Of or pertaining to the Pelasgians, their culture, etc.
etymology: From Ancient Greek Πελασγός (Pelasgós) + -ian, presumably based on a Pre-Greek ethnonym. Compare Egyptian pwrꜣsꜣtj, an ethnonym listed as one of the Sea Peoples attacking Egypt around 1190 BCE.

gloss: Of or relating to Phrygia, its people, or their culture.
etymology: From Latin Phrygiānus + English -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). gloss: A native or inhabitant of Phrygia.
etymology: From Latin Phrygiānus + English -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). gloss: The language of the Phrygian people.
